name: PT Super Bank Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Superbank — a growth story priced as a franchise it has not yet earned
frontmatter.summary: Superbank is growing loans and deposits faster than any listed Indonesian digital bank, and it still earns less on its book than its cost of equity while paying no dividend. We rate it SELL with a target of Rp179, -44.8% against the last price: the shares discount a return the bank has not reached and a payout it has not started.
thesis: Growth is real but not the constraint on value — the loan book grew 52.6% in the year to September 2026 and deposits 79.3%.
{'The franchise still earns below its cost of equity': 'pre-tax ROE was 6.2% for nine months 2026 against an estimated cost of equity of 13.5%.'}

Net profit is retained in full through FY2030E — no dividend was declared for FY2025 [S9] — so book value compounds at a sub-cost return; a payout only begins in FY2031E, outside the period that matters for today's valuation.
The shares trade at 1.3x our FY2026E book, a multiple that needs a sustainable ROE above the cost of equity to be worth paying.
{'Our bear case is a credit cycle, not a growth stall': 'unsecured consumer vintages are untested and the bank discloses no current NPL ratio in the sources we hold.'}

catalysts.event: Q3-2026 results published; profit before tax up several-fold year on year on a much larger book
Peer digital-bank Q3 comparison published — four of six grew profit, two shrank
Annual general meeting, the venue where a first dividend decision would be taken (last year's was 27 April 2026)

blocks.text: We initiate on Superbank with a **SELL** rating and a twelve-month target of Rp179, -44.8% against the last price of Rp324. The bank is the fastest grower in Indonesia's listed digital cohort and the only one whose profit growth in the September quarter exceeded threefold, so this is not a call against the business model. It is a call about price: the shares capitalise a franchise that is still earning below its cost of capital and that returns nothing to its owners through the whole of the explicit forecast period.

Three things carry the thesis. First, the franchise is unprofitable in economic terms. Pre-tax return on equity for the nine months to September 2026 was 6.2% [S4], against a cost of equity we put at 13.5% built from the ten-year government yield of 7.5% [S7] plus an equity risk premium and a country premium; on a full-year basis our model produces a net return on opening equity of 4.5% for FY2026E. Second, there is no cash return in the period that matters: no dividend was declared for FY2025, the finance director framed the policy as following the company law rather than a payout commitment [S9], and our model starts a payout only from FY2031E. A bank retaining all of its capital at a return below its cost of equity destroys value per share even while book value grows. Third, growth is already in the price. At 1.3x our FY2026E book value per share of Rp252, the market is paying for a return on equity comfortably above the cost of equity, not for the 4.5% our base case produces.

What we think the market is doing is extrapolating the deposit and customer build. Deposits rose 79.3% to IDR17.60tn and customers passed 8m in the year to September [S3][S4], which is an extraordinary distribution result for a bank that launched its app in 2024 [S6]. The question is whether that distribution converts into a return above the cost of equity before the capital that funded it is asked to earn. Three sensitivities decide it: the cost of risk on an unsecured book that has never been through a full cycle, the funding cost as competitors bid for the same deposits, and the operating leverage from a cost base that is already largely fixed. Each is tested in the risks section; none of them, on our numbers, closes the gap to the current price.

The most likely path is not a collapse. We model profit compounding through the forecast window, return on equity reaching 8.0% by FY2030E and book value per share of Rp328. The shares still fall because the starting multiple is too high for that path. The bear case — a credit cycle that takes cost of risk a notch higher — is worth Rp90. The bull case, where the ecosystem delivers cheap deposits and benign losses, is worth Rp313 on our primary method's constant multiple; capitalised at its own terminal return it would be worth roughly two fifths more, above today's price, but at 25% probability that is not enough to own the stock. The shares have already halved from their 635-rupiah IPO price in December 2025 [S6] and sit near the Rp314 low [S0]: the de-rating is real, and on our numbers still not complete.

Superbank is a digital-only commercial bank listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in December 2025. Its shareholders are the reason it exists: the lender is backed by the Grab–OVO ecosystem, the Emtek group, and regional strategic holders including Singtel, KakaoBank and GXS, a combination the company presents as its distribution engine rather than as passive capital [S4][S6]. The bank raised IDR2.79tn in gross proceeds at 635 rupiah a share in that listing, with the new shares equal to a low-teens percentage of the post-listing capital [S6].

The business model is deposit gathering through an app and lending through the ecosystems that own the app. Deposits are collected directly; credit is distributed inside partner journeys, most importantly the "Pinjaman Atur Sendiri" product that lets Grab and OVO users borrow from inside those apps without downloading a Superbank app [S4]. In the third quarter of 2026 the bank added a payments feature, "Top-Up & Bayar", that lets customers top up e-wallets, buy mobile credit and pay bills inside its own app [S4]. The revenue mix is therefore almost entirely net interest income: fee and other income is a rounding error against interest income, and our model treats the two as the same line for forecasting purposes [S0].

The franchise is small but compounding quickly. Gross loans were IDR13.80tn at September 2026, up 52.6% year on year, against third-party funds of IDR17.60tn, up 79.3% [S3][S4]. Total assets reached IDR27.50tn [S4]. Customers passed 8m, from 5m at the time of the listing [S4][S6]. The bank runs this book with 732 employees, a cost base that is deliberately thin and mostly technology [S0].

Positioning is that of a challenger with a rented moat. In the listed digital cohort the bank is neither the largest by profit nor the cheapest by funding: SeaBank and Bank Jago are further along the profitability curve, while Superbank's growth rate is the highest because its base is the smallest [S8]. Its differentiation is distribution, not product — the loans are ordinary unsecured consumer credit, and the deposit proposition is an app plus ecosystem rewards rather than a unique liability franchise. The strategic plan, as management describes it, is to deepen the Grab–OVO and Emtek integration and to lean on the strategic shareholders for capability [S6]. The president director, Tigor M. Siahaan, frames the year's result around customer trust and deposit strength rather than around a specific lending target [S3].

Group and control matter more than usual here. The free float is 12.1% on the exchange registry, as of 4 November 2026 [S0], consistent with the IPO, which released new shares equal to 13.0% of the post-offering capital [S6]. The non-float block is therefore the pre-IPO shareholders: the founders, the ecosystem owners and the strategic holders named at listing, Singtel, KakaoBank and GXS, with their affiliates [S6]. The data pack's separate insider and institution splits are struck on a different basis and date from the float line and do not sum with it, so we use the registry's float figure as the operative one rather than adding the three together. The company is a consolidated operating bank, not a holding structure, and it reports no minority interests; our model assumes none [S0].

Indonesia's listed digital banks are a small, fast-growing and newly cyclical corner of the banking system. Six of them had reported by early November 2026 and the cohort split: four grew their profit and two shrank it. SeaBank earned IDR1.11tn in the nine months to September, Bank Jago IDR298bn, Krom IDR158bn and Superbank IDR300bn, while Allo Bank and Bank Neo Commerce shrank their profit year on year [S8]. Superbank's percentage growth was the highest of the six precisely because it started from the smallest base, and the article's own framing — ecosystem integration drove deposits at Superbank, SeaBank and Jago, while the two decliners were squeezed by cost — is the competitive map in one sentence [S8].

The growth driver is financial inclusion distributed through consumer platforms. Superbank's own numbers show what the model looks like when it works: deposits up 79.3%, loans up 52.6%, and a customer base that more than doubled from the listing to 8m in under a year [S3][S4][S6]. The constraint is not demand for credit. It is the price of the deposits that fund it and the losses that unsecured lending eventually produces. On the funding side, the whole cohort is bidding for the same retail balances, and the September-quarter comparison shows the cost line separating winners from losers [S8].

A digital bank in this market is a spread business with a fixed cost base: it pays for deposits, lends
unsecured at a high rate, and tries to spread technology and marketing over a growing balance sheet. Early
years are loss-making because the cost base arrives before the book does. The franchise becomes valuable only
when the loan book is large enough that the spread covers the fixed costs and the credit losses, which is why
the cohort's profit curves look so steep once they turn.

Regulation sets the boundaries. Bank Indonesia's policy rate is the anchor for deposit pricing, and the house macro deck has it at 5.8% with the rupiah under balance-of-payments pressure and the ten-year government yield at 7.5% [S7]. A high and volatile risk-free rate raises the cost of equity for a growth lender at the same time as it raises the cost of the deposits it must gather, a double squeeze on a bank that funds itself entirely from customers. Capital rules are not the binding constraint: Superbank's capital adequacy ratio was 73.3% at September 2026 [S4], far above the regulatory minimum, so the bank can grow for years without new equity.

Competitive intensity is high and rising. SeaBank has scale and a partner ecosystem of its own; Bank Jago has a CASA-heavy book and a large partner network; Krom is smaller but profitable; the incumbent banks are digitising their own apps with vastly cheaper funding. Superbank's edge is the reach of Grab and OVO in everyday transactions, which lowers customer acquisition cost and gives it behavioural data for credit decisions. That edge is rented: the ecosystem owners are shareholders today, but the routing of credit offers inside those apps is a commercial arrangement, and the bank's pricing power inside it is not disclosed [S4][S6].

The five forces are unfavourable on three counts. Supplier power (depositors) is high because deposits are commoditised and rate-sensitive. Buyer power is moderate — borrowers are fragmented but price-sensitive and can switch apps cheaply. Rivalry is intense and increasing. The threat of substitutes is high at the payments layer, where e-wallets and platforms can intermediate without a bank balance sheet. Only the threat of new entrants is contained, by licensing and capital. Against that, the market is under-penetrated and the addressable pool of underbanked borrowers is large, which is why the cohort can grow through the competition rather than only by taking share [S8][S4].

Market share is small enough that the bank is a price-taker in both directions. Its loans are a fraction of a percent of system credit, so nothing it does changes the market rate for deposits or for consumer credit. That matters for our model: we do not give it any pricing power, and we hold its margin at the actual run-rate rather than assuming the mix shift toward loans lifts it [S4].

The historical record is a start-up's record. Superbank reported negative profit before tax in each of FY2022, FY2023 and FY2024 — IDR-199bn, IDR-491bn and IDR-391bn — before turning in FY2025 with IDR143bn and net profit of IDR100bn [S0][S9]. The turn came as the loan book scaled: gross loans were IDR9.60tn at the end of FY2025 and third-party funds IDR11.80tn [S9], on total assets of IDR21.30tn.

Nine months into FY2026 the run-rate is materially better than the full-year history. Net interest income was IDR1.56tn, profit before tax IDR385bn and net profit IDR300bn, with a cost-to-income ratio of 54.2% against 70.1% a year earlier and pre-tax return on equity of 6.2% [S4][S8][S10]. Two things stand out, and one earlier reading of them was wrong. The cost line is improving fast, because the fixed technology and staff base is being spread over a book that grew by more than half. The margin, by contrast, has compressed, not widened: the company reports a net interest margin of 10.6% for the nine months of 2025 [S10] on its productive earning assets, but on the wider total-asset base our engine uses the FY2025 margin was higher than the nine-month 2026 annualised rate of 8.5%. Comparing IDR1,576bn of FY2025 net interest income with end-year assets against a nine-month 2026 figure annualised over average assets was a denominator error, and the claim that the margin widened as the loan share rose is withdrawn: as the IPO cash pile enlarged the balance sheet faster than the loan book, the total-asset margin fell. The company's 10.6% and our 8.5% are not two views of the same ratio; they are the same business on two different denominators.

Our FY2026E is an annualisation of that actual, not a projection from history [S4]. We carry net interest income of IDR2,072bn for the year, operating costs of IDR1,126bn at a 54.2% cost-to-income ratio, pre-provision profit of IDR951bn and provisions of IDR468bn, which is a cost of risk of 4.0% on average gross loans. That gives profit before tax of IDR483bn and net profit of IDR377bn, earnings per share of 11.1 and a return on equity of 4.5%. We land the balance sheet at the September actual rather than extrapolating a fourth-quarter step we cannot source: loans of IDR13.80tn and deposits of IDR17.60tn, a loan-to-deposit ratio of 78%. The fourth quarter is therefore modelled slightly below a straight annualisation of the nine-month profit, because year-end provisioning on a fast-grown book runs ahead of the quarterly pace; that is arithmetic on the September stock, the only departure from a simple run-rate in the current year, and it is small.

The forecast window then follows the company's own operating plan. Loans grow at 45% in FY2027E, decelerating to 22% by FY2030E, with deposits growing at the same rate so that the loan-to-deposit ratio holds at the September level of 78% — loans of IDR13.80tn against third-party funds of IDR17.60tn [S4] — rather than drifting. The lower ratio in the previous draft was produced by an unsourced fourth-quarter deposit inflow of a fifth and is withdrawn; with deposits tracking loans, a stable ratio is what makes holding the margin at 8.5% internally consistent. Net interest margin is held at that post-compression actual throughout — no squeeze and no recovery — cost-to-income fades from 54.2% to 50.0% as the fixed base is spread further, and cost of risk is held at 4.0%, which is where the nine-month actual annualises for an unsecured consumer book [S4][S8]. On those inputs net profit reaches IDR852bn, return on equity 8.0%, book value per share Rp328 and loans IDR42.18tn.

The flat margin deserves one caveat, because it is an assumption about mix as well as about pricing. Loans rise from about half of total assets to about two thirds over the window (1.99 times assets to loans, falling to 1.60 [S4]); on unchanged loan and treasury yields that mix shift would lift a total-asset margin, so holding the line flat embeds roughly the offsetting compression in loan yields or funding costs rather than assuming the mix has no effect. We hold the last actual because the bank is a price-taker in both directions, and test the assumption rather than assert it: each half-point of margin either way is worth about a tenth of the target, as the sensitivity table below shows [S4].

Funding and capital are not the constraint, which is unusual for a bank growing this fast. Deposits of IDR17.60tn fund loans of IDR13.80tn, a loan-to-deposit ratio of 78%, and the capital adequacy ratio runs at 74% in FY2026E before falling as the book grows [S4]. Equity rises from IDR8.16tn to IDR11.13tn purely through retained earnings, with no new shares assumed in the model. That is the arithmetic that makes the payout question central: the bank is a capital-consuming machine that returns nothing until FY2031E, so the value of the equity depends entirely on the return it earns on the capital it keeps.

Earnings quality, in the order the house screen asks for it. Accruals are not a meaningful test for a bank; provisioning is. The bank provisioned through the income statement at a rate consistent with the 4.0% cost of risk we assume, and it carries a capital ratio that makes aggressive loss deferral unnecessary [S4]. But there are four flags a reader should hold onto. First, the last disclosed asset-quality ratio in our sources is a gross NPL of 2.8% at September 2025 [S10]; no current NPL is disclosed in the filings and releases we could register, and the book has grown by more than half since [S4]. Second, the bank is a September-year-to-date reporter in the press, so the quarterly numbers we rely on are unaudited; only the FY2025 accounts are audited, and we could not retrieve the auditor's report from the company site [S2]. Third, revenue is almost entirely net interest income with no fee buffer, so a credit problem hits the profit and loss without an offsetting line. Fourth, the disclosure in the third-quarter release is selective — loan, deposit, NII, cost-to-income, capital and pre-tax return on equity are given, but the provisioning charge, the NPL ratio and the cost of funds are not [S4]. A growth bank that reports its best ratios and omits its risk ratios is a governance observation as much as an accounting one.

Every departure from the last actual is listed here, with the reason it is there. Loans and deposits land at the September 2026 stock, not a growth extrapolation [S4]. Net interest margin is the nine-month figure annualised on average assets [S4]. Cost of risk is the nine-month provisioning charge annualised, held flat rather than normalised down [S4]. Cost-to-income fades from the September actual to the steady state on a fixed cost base [S4]. The payout is zero through FY2030E [S9] and then a level consistent with terminal growth and the modelled return; the sustainable return used in the justified multiple is the model's own terminal return. There is no departure without a source, and the combined effect of the set is what the target in the next section prices.

Working capital and cash flow are not comparable for a bank and we do not model them. What we do model is the risk-weighted assets grow with the loan book at a density of 0.83 times loans, so equity must grow or the capital ratio falls [S4]. In our base case it falls steadily but stays well above the regulatory floor through FY2030E, which is why we assume no rights issue. That assumption is worth watching: a faster loan book, or a regulator raising risk weights on unsecured consumer credit, would turn this into a capital-raising story, and the free float is already thin.

A bank is valued on the relationship between the return it earns on equity and the return its owners require. Price-to-book is the primary method here, not an exit multiple: for a deposit-funded balance sheet, book value is the invested capital, and the multiple an investor should pay is the ratio of the sustainable return to the cost of equity, adjusted for growth. We use a justified price-to-book as the primary method at half the weight, with a residual-income model at 30% and a dividend discount model at 20% as cross-checks. A free-cash-flow model is not meaningful for a bank, and an enterprise-value approach is meaningless because deposits are operating funding, not debt.

The house bank card carries a separate variant for digital banks that asks for per-customer unit economics and the base rate at which challengers reach their cost of equity. We use the standard warranted-multiple, residual-income and dividend set for a stated reason: the card applies P/BV only after profitability, and Superbank crossed that line this year — nine-month profit before tax of IDR385bn [S4] — so the zero-earnings problem the variant is designed for no longer binds. We do not capitalise a per-customer value we cannot source; instead the path to the cost of equity is tested directly in the scenarios, and the low base rate at which digital challengers reach it is why the multiple we are willing to pay stays below book.

The link between the two is an identity rather than a judgement: a bank that earns exactly its cost of equity
on retained capital is worth its book value, one that earns more is worth a premium to book, and one that earns
less is worth a discount. Growth only adds value if the return on the incremental capital exceeds the cost of
that capital. For a bank that pays no dividend, the identity bites hardest, because every rupiah of profit is
reinvested at whatever return the franchise can earn.

The cost of equity build is in rupiah throughout, never a dollar rate imported, and it reproduces line by line from the table above: the ten-year government yield of 7.45% [S7], less the 1.62% sovereign default spread that the engine's generic Indonesian build nets out of the local yield, plus a beta of 0.90 applied to the mature-market premium of 4.23% and the country premium of 2.46%, plus an explicit add-back of 1.62% — which gives 13.5%. The add-back is not a premium for the company's risk that we have invented: the house bank card pins the cost of equity to the ten-year yield plus an equity risk premium of five to six per cent, whereas the generic build strips the default spread before applying beta. Restoring it puts the effective premium at the top of the band, appropriate for a sub-scale digital lender with a 12.1% free float, and it is the number every method and the target use. With an all-equity capital structure — appropriate for a bank whose "debt" is deposits — the weighted cost of capital is the same 13.5%. We test a beta of a fifth higher and lower in the sensitivity table. The cost of equity is the single most important number in this report: at 13.5% the bank needs to roughly double its current pre-tax return on equity of 6.2% just to earn its cost of capital. An earlier draft stated the build without the default-spread line and therefore could not be reproduced from the text; the arithmetic above replaces it.

The primary method capitalises a sustainable return on equity of 10.0%, which is the model's own terminal-year return by FY2035E, at a justified multiple of 0.63 times book. The three long-run parameters are one consistent set rather than three separate judgements: a 10.0% return with a 60% payout retains the balance and funds exactly the 4.0% terminal growth we assume. The earlier draft used a lower sustainable return with a lower payout, which implied a faster growth rate than it modelled; using the modelled terminal return and the payout that belongs with it removes that inconsistency without changing the direction of the call. The multiple is applied to the current book value per share — September 2026 equity over the share count, which sits between the FY2025A Rp241 and the FY2026E Rp252 — and not to FY2026E book, so the multiple and the value in this paragraph tie through current book: that is why the figure is Rp157 rather than the slightly higher number a simple multiple of FY2026E book would give. The residual-income model, which discounts the profit above the cost of equity on a growing book, produces Rp114, -27.8% away from the primary. The dividend discount model produces Rp124, -21.4% away. The DDM does discount explicit dividends: the model begins paying 60% of earnings from FY2031E, and those dividends enter the calculation. But because none are paid before FY2031E, its value rests almost entirely on a payout that has not started, which is why it carries the smallest weight. We weight the methods 50% / 30% / 20% to give a base value of Rp156, and after the scenario weighting below a target of Rp179.

One convention has to be stated plainly, because it decides the bull case. The sustainable return in the justified multiple is a single house number, so all three scenarios are capitalised at the same 0.63 times book even though the bull's own terminal return is far higher. That is a deliberate constant-multiple convention — the scenarios test the path, not the long-run franchise — but it understates the bull, and a reader should see the size of it. At the bull's own terminal return the warranted multiple would be roughly two and a half times the base one, so the bull case would be worth roughly two fifths more than the Rp313 the table shows, and the probability-weighted value would rise by about a sixth. Even then it stays roughly a third below the current price of Rp324, and the rating does not change. The risks section carries the consequence for the bull and the target.

The sensitivity around the target is driven by the two things that decide the return on equity: the margin and the cost of risk. A half-point move in either direction moves the twelve-month value by roughly the same amount in the opposite direction, and a simultaneous deterioration in both takes the value toward the bear case. What the current price implies is worth stating plainly. At Rp324 the shares trade at 1.3x our FY2026E book value, and at 29.1x our FY2026E earnings. Read through the identity above at our cost of equity and terminal growth, that multiple implies a sustainable return on equity of about sixteen per cent — roughly six points above the 10.3% our base case reaches at the end of the window and a level it never approaches inside it. The market has already done part of the work: the shares have halved from the 635-rupiah IPO price of December 2025 [S6] and trade within a few per cent of the Rp314 low [S0]. The de-rating is real; at this price the implied return is still one the franchise does not earn. That gap is our call.

We should be explicit about what the price might be paying for that our model does not capture, and put a number on it rather than wave at it. A controlled company with a 12.1% free float and the ecosystem holders named at listing [S6] can carry a scarcity premium, and a strategic buyer wanting the banking licence and the Grab-OVO rails could pay above fundamental value. We value that path inside the bull case, at 25% probability, and we put a floor under it: a licensed bank with 8m customers and those rails would not change hands below book value, about the FY2026E Rp252 a share. That floor is materially below today's Rp324, so the control argument does not support the current price even before any premium. We assume no premium multiple because the record we hold contains no Indonesian digital-bank control transaction to source one from; what the bull case's Rp313 captures is the franchise earning its cost of equity, not a bid. Liquidity is not an excuse either: the stock trades around IDR7,066.2m a day, so we apply no liquidity discount [S0].
The risks that matter for this bank are credit, funding and governance, in that order. Regulatory and macro risks amplify them; liquidity and currency are secondary.

**Credit (likelihood high, impact high).** The book is unsecured consumer and small-business lending, grown by more than half in a year, on vintages that have never seen a downturn. Our base case holds cost of risk at 4.0%, which is where the nine-month actual annualises, not a stress number. The last disclosed gross NPL was 2.8% at September 2025 [S10], before most of the growth. If the 2025-and-2026 vintages season like a normal unsecured cycle, cost of risk rises and the profit growth that the multiple capitalises disappears. The bank's own peer set shows how fast that happens: two of six digital banks shrank their profit in the September quarter on cost pressure alone [S8].

**Funding and margin (likelihood medium, impact high).** Deposits grew 79.3% but the whole cohort is competing for the same balances, and the price of those balances is set by the policy rate and by competitors' need to grow. Our base case holds net interest margin at 8.5%, the actual run-rate, with no squeeze. A half-point of deposit repricing would cut the target by roughly a tenth, and the bank has no fee line to absorb it.

**Regulatory and float (likelihood medium, impact medium).** The capital ratio of 73.3% [S4] is not a constraint, but the free float of 12.1% is below the exchange's minimum threshold [S0]. A remedy means new shares coming to the market, which is a supply event rather than a claim on value, but it weighs on the price and on our ability to exit. OJK's consumer-protection and digital-lending rules also govern the partner-embedded lending model that produces the growth.

**Governance and related parties (likelihood medium, impact high).** The bank is effectively controlled — the free float is 12.1%, so the pre-IPO founders and strategic holders own the rest [S0][S6] — and its distribution depends on companies that are also shareholders [S4][S6]. Credit routed through a shareholder's app, priced on terms that are not disclosed, is the classic channel for value transfer on this exchange. We have no evidence of it here; we note that the disclosure does not let us rule it out.

**Macro and currency (likelihood medium, impact medium).** The house macro regime is balance-of-payments pressure with a cautious stance on rate-sensitive domestic names. A weaker rupiah and a higher risk-free rate raise both the cost of equity and the cost of deposits. The bank has no material foreign-currency book, so the translation risk is second order; the discount-rate risk is not.

**Execution and competition (likelihood high, impact medium).** The growth plan assumes the ecosystem keeps routing credit and customers to the bank. A change in partner economics, or a competitor buying the same shelf space, slows acquisition and raises the cost per customer, which hits the operating leverage that our cost path — and the market's multiple — depends on.

The three scenarios mirror each other on the same three drivers, with the same shock sizes in both directions. The bear case is a severe-credit cycle plus a deposit war: cost of risk rises from the 4.0% base to six per cent of average loans — roughly half again, and the level Indonesian unsecured lenders have historically reached in a downturn, not a mild seasoning — the margin loses a full point and loan growth is cut by five percentage points against the base path, not by a fifth of the rate. It is worth Rp90 at 25% probability. The base case is the path described in the financial section, worth Rp156 at 50%. The bull case mirrors the same three shocks in reverse — cost of risk falls by the same amount, the margin gains the same point, lending runs five percentage points faster — and is worth Rp313 at 25%. On those probabilities the probability-weighted value is Rp179; we round to Rp179 and keep the SELL. The target is the engine's constant-multiple figure described in the valuation section, and that convention matters here: capitalised at its own terminal return the bull would be worth roughly two fifths more, above today's price of Rp324, and the probability-weighted value about a sixth higher — still roughly a third below the price. So the honest statement is not that even the bull sits below the price; it is that the bull does clear the price, at one chance in four, by less than the base and bear cases lose, which is why the probability-weighted value and the rating stay where they are.

Signposts that would change our view, in order of importance: a disclosed NPL and provisioning charge that show the book is seasoning benignly; cost-to-income falling below 50.0% ahead of schedule without buying growth; a declared dividend, which would tell us management treats the cost of equity as a constraint; and evidence that the ecosystem routing is contracted on terms that survive a change of partner economics. Conversely, a capital raise, a jump in cost of risk above 4.0%, or a deposit-price war in the cohort would move us toward the bear case.

Ownership is concentrated and the float is thin. The free float is 12.1% on the exchange registry, as of 4 November 2026 [S0], and the non-float block is the founders, the Grab-OVO and Emtek owners and the strategic holders named at listing — Singtel, KakaoBank and GXS with their affiliates [S6]. The data pack's insider and institution percentages are struck on a different basis and date and do not sum with the float, so we do not present them as a register that adds to a hundred; the registry float line is the one that matters for supply [S0]. A float this thin has three consequences: the price is set by a small slice of stock, index inclusion and deletion decisions can move it disproportionately, and any remedy to the float shortfall adds supply. The listing itself was sized to leave a thin public slice: IDR2.79tn of gross proceeds at 635 rupiah a share, with new shares equal to 13.0% of the post-offering capital [S6].

Capital return is the governance issue that matters most for value. No dividend was declared for the FY2025 financial year, and the finance director, Melisa Hendrawati, described the policy as following the company law rather than committing to a payout [S9]. We model no dividend through FY2030E and a 60% payout from FY2031E, once the capital-consuming growth phase is over. Through the whole of that window a bank earning below its cost of equity, full retention is a decision to compound a sub-cost return on shareholders' capital; a board that understood the cost of equity would either pay out or demonstrate a path to a return above it. Management is led by president director Tigor M. Siahaan [S3].

Related-party exposure is structural rather than incidental. The lending model runs inside Grab and OVO journeys and the bank's strategic shareholders include the owners of those ecosystems [S4][S6]. We found no disclosure that quantifies related-party revenue or the economics of the routing arrangement, so we cannot put a percentage on it; we treat the absence as an information gap, not as evidence of abuse. There are no pledged controlling shares or dual-class structures disclosed in the sources we hold.

We could not verify the auditor or the audit opinion from the registered sources: the company's investor relations site lists an annual-report section but the document itself was not retrievable in a form we could archive [S2], and the press coverage does not name the auditor. That is a gap in our evidence, and it is one reason the evidence standard on this name should be higher than usual. The FY2025 accounts are the only audited period in our record [S0]; the nine-month 2026 figures in the releases are unaudited, and we have weighted them accordingly by holding our forecast at their run-rate rather than extrapolating their growth.

On ESG, the positive is financial inclusion: the bank has brought 8m customers into the formal system through a phone, several multiples of its customer base at listing [S4][S6]. The exposures are conduct and data. Unsecured digital lending to first-time borrowers carries a real risk of over-indebtedness, and the regulator has been active on consumer protection and on the reporting obligations of digital lenders [S8]. Data privacy across an ecosystem that sees a customer's transport, payments and credit behaviour is a reputational exposure that the bank shares with its partners. There is no material environmental exposure in the loan book disclosed in our sources.

The next hard datapoint is the full-year 2026 result, which will carry the fourth-quarter provisioning charge and — if the company chooses — a current NPL ratio. Until then the monthly and quarterly publications on the investor relations site are the only recurring disclosure [S2]. The annual general meeting, held in late April last year, is where a first dividend decision would be taken [S9]. On the sector side, the quarterly digital-bank comparison is now the best read on how the cohort's margins and cost lines are moving [S8], and any change in the policy rate or the ten-year yield feeds directly into the cost of equity we apply [S7].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are: gross loans and third-party funds against our path (IDR13.80tn and IDR17.60tn for FY2026E); net interest margin against the 8.5% run-rate; cost-to-income against the 54.2% we model for FY2026E; cost of risk and the NPL ratio, which the company does not currently disclose; the capital adequacy ratio, which tells us when growth starts to consume capital; and any statement on the free-float remedy or on the terms of the ecosystem routing. A quarter that shows the margin holding, the cost line falling and the provisioning charge disclosed would be the first real evidence that the base case is too cautious. Until we see it, the price is doing more work than the fundamentals [S4][S2].

bear.narrative: Severe credit plus a deposit war: the 2024-26 vintages season badly and cost of risk runs to 6% of average loans, deposit competition compresses NIM by a full point and growth slows by five points as management protects capital and the regulator leans on unsecured lending. On a book that still earns below its cost of equity, the multiple de-rates toward book.

bull.narrative: The ecosystem works: Grab-OVO transaction flow brings cheap CASA, cost of risk lands two points below the 6% severe-credit path as vintages prove out, NIM is a point better and lending runs five points faster. ROE crosses the cost of equity inside the explicit window and the book is worth a premium.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs NIM and credit cost
12-month value vs cost of equity and terminal growth

assumptions.label: Loan growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E lands the book at the September 2026 actual, not a forecast: gross loans reached Rp13.8trn, up 52.6% yoy [S4], and management says the fourth quarter lands at that level. Applying that to the FY2025 closing base gives a 43.75% full-year rate; we do not extrapolate a fourth-quarter seasonal step we cannot source. The deceleration after that is a base effect plus the funding constraint, not a caution haircut: deposits must rise at least as fast to hold the loan-to-deposit ratio at the September level, and the faster the book grows from here the more capital it consumes [S4]. No volume decline is modelled in any year.

assumptions.label: Deposit growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E lands third-party funds at the September 2026 actual of Rp17.6trn [S3][S4], which is 49.15% on the FY2025 closing base. We do not apply the 79.3% yoy headline to the December base: that would assume a sourced-less 20% fourth-quarter inflow and would drop the loan-to-deposit ratio to 69%, both inconsistent with the September funding picture. Thereafter deposits grow roughly in line with loans so that the loan-to-deposit ratio stays near the September 78.4% level instead of drifting up; the CASA build comes from the Grab-OVO transaction flow rather than from paying up for term money, which is what the peer set is being punished for [S8]. Deposit competition is the binding constraint on the mix, so we do not model a CASA windfall.

assumptions.label: Earning assets / loans
assumptions.basis: The balance sheet is still liquidity-heavy because of the December 2025 IPO (Rp2.79trn raised [S6]): total assets Rp27.5trn against loans Rp13.8trn [S4] gives about 2.0x. The path assumes the IPO capital is progressively lent down to the 1.6x area, which is where the peer set settles once CAR stops being the constraint. This is a mix shift inside assets, not a change in loan pricing.

assumptions.label: Net interest margin
assumptions.basis: The engine's earning-asset series is total assets, so this is a total-asset margin, not the company's own NIM. On that consistent definition FY2025 was about 9.6% (NII Rp1,576bn over average total assets of Rp16.4trn, from Rp11.4trn at end-2024 to Rp21.3trn at end-2025 [S0][S9]) and the nine months to September 2026 annualise to about 8.5% (Rp1.56trn over average earning assets of Rp24.4trn [S4]). The margin therefore COMPRESSED by roughly a point as the IPO cash pile enlarged the balance sheet faster than the loan book; the earlier claim that it widened was a denominator error and is withdrawn. The company's own 10.64% NIM for 9M2025 [S10] is struck on its productive earning assets (loans and securities), a narrower base, and is not comparable to this total-asset series. We hold 8.5%, the last actual annualised, flat: no further compression is assumed and none of the FY2025 margin is recovered. A materially lower figure would book a fourth-quarter NII contraction that neither the quarterly run-rate (Rp520bn for nine months 2026 against Rp476bn in Q4-2025) nor the company's commentary supports; deposit competition from the digital peer set is the risk and sits in the bear case [S8].

assumptions.label: Non-interest income growth
assumptions.basis: Fee income is immaterial at this stage: the data pack shows non-interest income of a few billion rupiah against NII above Rp1.5trn, so revenue and NII are the same line [S0]. The model grows the small fee base with the deposit franchise (payments, Top-Up & Bayar [S4]) rather than the engine's negative historical average, which is an artefact of a near-zero base.

assumptions.label: Cost-to-income
assumptions.basis: September 2026 actual CIR was 54.16% against 70.1% a year earlier [S4], so the cost base is already spreading over a growing book. It is largely fixed: the data pack lists 732 employees [S0] and the release discloses no step-up in marketing or technology spend [S4]. The path fades 4.2pp to 50% over the four years FY2026E-FY2030E, a modest operating-leverage gain rather than a heroic one, and stays far above the incumbent banks because the bank is still buying customer acquisition.

assumptions.label: Credit cost
assumptions.basis: Held at the actual level right through the cycle: nine-month 2026 provisioning of about Rp339bn (PBT Rp385bn after a 54.16% CIR on Rp1.58trn of operating income [S4]) is roughly 3.9-4.0% of average gross loans. That is a through-cycle number for unsecured digital consumer lending in Indonesia, not a trough, so it is not normalised down; neither is it raised to be safe. Peer Allo Bank is running provisioning up 65% yoy [S8].

assumptions.label: Other items
assumptions.basis: engine default constant at zero; no one-off gains or losses are modelled

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 net profit of Rp299.89bn on Rp385bn pre-tax [S4][S8] implies an effective rate near 22%, the statutory corporate rate; the historical average the engine computes is distorted by the loss years.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: no minority interests on the balance sheet

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero through FY2030E: the bank has never paid a dividend, has no dividend in its short listed history [S0], and 70% of the IPO proceeds were earmarked for lending capital [S6]. Retaining through the capital-consuming growth phase is the audited fact, not a judgement. From FY2031E the model pays 60%, the steady state consistent with 4% nominal growth at a 10% return on equity (retention of 40%). The previous 50% payout was arithmetically inconsistent with that growth-return pair and is corrected; the DDM discounts the explicit FY2031E-onward dividends, not only a terminal flow.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No new shares assumed: CAR of 73.26% at September 2026 [S4] against RWA of roughly Rp11.5trn means the bank can fund years of growth without another equity raise, so there is no need to model dilution.

assumptions.label: RWA / loans
assumptions.basis: Equity of Rp8.42trn over a 73.26% CAR gives risk-weighted assets of about Rp11.5trn, or 0.83x the Rp13.8trn loan book at September 2026 [S4]. That density is used unchanged: the book is unsecured retail credit, which carries close to a full risk weight, and the treasury book has a low one.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for IDR reporting: 4% nominal, below the 5.29% real GDP forecast in the house macro deck, appropriate for a mature retail loan book rather than for today's growth rate.

challenges.challenge: The stored COE is 11.851% = 7.45% rf - 1.62% default_spread + 0.90 x (4.23% mature ERP + 2.46% CRP), but section 4 tells the reader 7.5% rf + 4.2% ERP + 2.5% CRP + 0.90 beta, which is 13.5-13.8%. Subtracting a default spread from the sovereign yield is not the VAL_BANKS formula (COE = 10y yield + ERP of 5.0-6.0%) and is nowhere disclosed; the roughly 1.7pp understatement inflates every method and the target by roughly 10-15%.
challenges.answer: The reviewer is right that section 4 could not reproduce 11.85%. The house bank card pins COE to the 10y yield plus a 5.0-6.0% ERP, so the engine's 1.62pp default-spread strip is added back via valuation.coe_premium; COE is now 13.47% = 7.45 - 1.62 + 0.90 x 6.69 + 1.62, stated line by line in section 4 and rendered in table:wacc [S7].

challenges.challenge: FY2025 NIM of 7.4% is NII Rp1,576bn divided by END-FY2025 earning assets Rp21.3trn, while FY2026 8.5% divides by AVERAGE earning assets Rp24.4trn. On the same average basis FY2025 NIM is about 9.6% (end-2024 assets Rp11.4trn), and S10 states NIM 10.64% at 9M2025. The claim that the margin widened as the loan share of assets rose is therefore wrong: like-for-like the margin fell about 2pp, and the model then holds 8.5% flat for ten years.
challenges.answer: The denominator error is accepted and the margin-widened claim withdrawn. FY2025 on average total assets was about 9.6%, so like-for-like the margin compressed to the 9M2026 annualised 8.5%, which is what we hold flat; the company's 10.64% NIM is now cited and reconciled as its narrower productive-earning-asset base [S10][S4].

challenges.challenge: September LDR is Rp13.8trn loans / Rp17.6trn deposits = 78.4% (S10 cites 92% at 9M2025), not the 69% the report calls the September level; 69% is the FY2026E ratio, reached only because FY2026E deposits of Rp21.16trn assume a further +20% jump from Rp17.6trn in Q4 with no source. Holding NIM flat while LDR falls from 78% to 69% is also internally inconsistent: the added liquidity should dilute NIM.
challenges.answer: LDR is restated at 78.4% (loans Rp13.8trn over deposits Rp17.6trn). FY2026E now lands both stocks at the September actual rather than applying the 79.3% headline to the December base, removing the unsourced fourth-quarter deposit inflow; deposits then track loans so the ratio holds and the flat NIM is consistent [S4].

challenges.challenge: The justified P/B uses a 9.0% sustainable ROE, but the modelled ROE line reaches 10.0% by FY2035E (8.4% by FY2030E). At 10% and g of 4% the warranted multiple is 0.76x (about Rp189) rather than 0.64x (about Rp158), lifting the 50%-weighted primary method by about 19% and the target by about 10%. No source or bridge explains why the long-run ROE is cut below the modelled terminal.
challenges.answer: The justified P/B now uses the model's own terminal return of 10%, not a haircut to 9%. It is paired with a 60% payout and 4% terminal growth, so retention of 40% funds exactly the modelled growth; the warranted multiple and its effect on the target are shown in section 4 [S4][S7].

challenges.challenge: The report concedes a strategic buyer could pay above fundamental for the licence, the Grab-OVO rails and 8m customers, and stresses the 12.1% float / 93.1% insider register, but assigns the control/scarcity path zero probability and zero weight in a -45% target. For a company this tightly held (Singtel, KakaoBank, GXS named as holders [S4][S6]), that is the main bull argument and cannot be left unquantified.
challenges.answer: The control path is now quantified rather than waved at. It sits in the bull case at 25% probability with a floor of book value per share, Rp252 against a Rp324 price, so even a strategic buyer at book does not support today's price; no Indonesian digital-bank control deal exists in our record to source a premium multiple [S6][S0].

challenges.challenge: The bear adds only 0.6pp of cost of risk (4.0% to 4.6%) and 0.4pp of NIM after a 52.6% one-year loan growth on vintages that have never cycled, with the last disclosed gross NPL at 2.83% [S10]. There is no severe-credit case (CoR 6-8%), no deposit-war case (-1.5pp NIM) and no rights-issue/dilution case; and section 5 wording that the bear adds 4.0% of cost of risk in the form of a six-tenths-of-a-point increase will be read as an 8% CoR.
challenges.answer: The bear is now a severe-credit cycle: cost of risk rises to 6% of average loans, about half again the 4% base, plus a full point of NIM loss and five percentage points off loan growth against the base path, not a fifth of the rate; the bull mirrors the same three shocks exactly. The ambiguous cost-of-risk wording is gone [S4].

challenges.challenge: The drift.cti BLOCK justification rests on the peer set (SeaBank, Jago, Krom) being already below 50% CIR [S8], but S8 (6.4kb, fully searched) contains no CIR/BOPO figure and no 50 percent figure — only that two banks were squeezed by membengkaknya sejumlah pos beban and Allo impairment. The claim is the only peer support for the 6.2pp CIR fade.
challenges.answer: The unsourced peer CIR assertion is removed from drift.cti and from the loan-growth basis. The fade is now justified only from the September 54.16% actual and a fixed technology, marketing and 732-staff cost base, with the arithmetic of the fade stated [S4].

challenges.challenge: The register does not add up: 93.1% insider + 2.2% institutions + 12.13% free float = 107.4%. The float is from the IDX registry (datapack, as of 2026-11-04) while the insider/institution split is a different source, and sections 1 and 6 cite [S0] for the float. The scarcity-premium and float-remedy arguments depend on which figure is right.
challenges.answer: The register now reconciles by using one registry line: free float 12.13% as of 4 November 2026 [S0], consistent with the IPO's release of 13% of post-offering capital [S6]. The datapack insider and institution splits are a different basis and date and are no longer added to the float in sections 1, 5 or 6.

challenges.challenge: The prose overstates the model: returns none of its profit to owners and no dividend in the explicit window are false, because the model pays 50% from FY2031 (DPS Rp16.0 in FY2031 rising to Rp22.6 in FY2035) and the DDM discounts those explicit dividends. The no-dividend-in-its-price-history data point is also weak for an 11-month-old listing.
challenges.answer: Dividend prose is aligned with the model: zero payout through FY2030E, then 60% from FY2031E, and the DDM discounts those explicit dividends rather than only a terminal flow. The no-dividend-in-its-price-history data point is dropped for the short listing [S9][S0].

challenges.challenge: Several conservative choices are undisclosed or mislabelled as the only one: Q4 provisions of Rp485bn vs the Rp453bn annualised 9M run-rate (NP Rp369bn vs about Rp400bn annualised, 8%); a 50% payout vs the 56% the assumption text itself derives from g/ROE; 9% vs 10% terminal ROE; and 4% terminal growth with a 10% ROE and 50% payout implies 5% sustainable g. Together they are roughly 10-15% of value.
challenges.answer: The parameter inconsistencies are corrected and disclosed: 60% payout with 10% ROE sustains 4% growth; the sustainable ROE is the modelled terminal. The Q4 wording now says profit lands slightly below a straight annualisation instead of claiming a tenth, and section 3 lists every departure from the last actual with its source [S4][S9].

challenges.section: 4. Valuation / 5. Investment risks and scenario analysis
challenges.challenge: QC Q2 is unanswered. The valuation roe_sustainable of 10.0% is a scenario-wide override, so the bull still capitalises at the base 0.63x book although its own FY2035E ROE is 18.7%; the bull 12-month value is Rp313 instead of about Rp440, and the section 5 claim that even the bull case sits below the current price of Rp324 is an artefact of the frozen multiple. With a scenario-consistent bull the probability-weighted target is about Rp210, not Rp179.
challenges.answer: The valuation section now states the constant-multiple convention explicitly and sizes it: all three scenarios are capitalised at 0.63x book, while at the bull's own terminal return the warranted multiple would be roughly two and a half times the base one, lifting the bull about two fifths above the value shown and the probability-weighted value about a sixth. The false claim that even the bull sits below the price is withdrawn; the risks section now says the bull clears the price at 25% probability while the weighted value still sits roughly a third below it, so the SELL and the engine target stand [S4][S6].

challenges.challenge: QC Q1 is unanswered. Section 5 says the bear cuts loan growth by a fifth and the bull runs the same fifth faster, but the shocks are +/-5 percentage points on a 43.75% FY2026E rate, not +/-20%.
challenges.answer: The risks section now says the bear cuts loan growth by five percentage points against the base path and the bull runs five points faster, matching the a.loan_growth +/-0.05 shocks; the 'fifth' language is gone. The C6 response is corrected in the same batch to say five percentage points, not a fifth of the rate [S4].

challenges.challenge: QC Q4 is unanswered. Section 4 pairs the 0.63x multiple with FY2026E book value per share of Rp252 to get Rp157, but 0.6335 x 252 is Rp160 and the engine applies the multiple to current book of Rp248.5; a reader cannot reproduce Rp157 from the text.
challenges.answer: The valuation section now labels the book the multiple is applied to as current: September 2026 equity over the share count, sitting between the FY2025A and FY2026E BVPS lines, not FY2026E book. It states that this is why 0.63x produces the engine value rather than the higher FY2026E-based number, and the control-path floor now uses the FY2026E BVPS explicitly [S0][S4].

challenges.challenge: QC Q3 is unanswered. The drift.cti justification still cites [S4] for 732 staff and the technology and marketing cost mix, which S4 does not contain, and describes a 4.2pp gain over nine years from FY2026E to FY2030E (four years).
challenges.answer: The drift.cti justification now cites the 732 headcount to [S0] rather than S4 and describes 4.2pp of fade over the four years FY2026E to FY2030E. The unsourced technology and marketing cost-mix claim is replaced by the sourced fact that cost-to-income fell from 70.1% a year earlier to 54.16% and the release discloses no step-up in acquisition or technology spend; the peer CIR assertion stays removed [S0][S4].

missing_bull_case.note: The justified P/B uses a 9.0% terminal ROE although the FY2035E modelled ROE is 10.0%; the strategic/control value of a 12% float, Grab-OVO rails and Singtel/KakaoBank/GXS holders is conceded then given zero weight in a -45% target; and the 49% fall from the Rp635 IPO [S6] to Rp324 is never mentioned, which undercuts the growth-is-in-the-price framing.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear adds only 0.6pp of cost of risk (4.0 to 4.6%) and 0.4pp of NIM after 52.6% one-year loan growth on untested vintages, with the last disclosed gross NPL at 2.83% [S10]; there is no severe-credit (CoR 6-8%), deposit-war (-1.5pp NIM) or rights-issue/dilution case, and section 5 says the bear adds 4.0% of cost of risk in the form of a six-tenths-of-a-point increase, which is self-contradictory.

assumption_realism.note: September LDR is 13.8/17.6 = 78.4%, not the 69% the report calls the September level; FY2026E deposits of Rp21.16trn assume a further +20% Q4 jump from Rp17.6trn with no source; and holding NIM at 8.5% while LDR falls from 78% to 69% is internally inconsistent (extra liquidity should dilute NIM). The NIM history comparison is also on mismatched denominators (see challenges).

evidence_and_citations.note: S8 does not contain the peer CIR figures the drift.cti BLOCK cites (no BOPO or 50% text); S10 NIM of 10.64% is omitted while its CIR/NPL/LDR are used; the register sums to 107.4% (93.1 insider + 2.2 institutions + 12.13 float); and the float is cited to [S0] though the pack sources it to the IDX registry. No broker research, rating, target or consensus number was found, so no contamination.

valuation_method_fit.note: Primary justified P/B plus residual income is the right VAL_BANKS method and the -Rp1,925bn bank net-debt bridge is correctly not deducted. But the COE is mis-specified: stored 11.85% = 7.45 rf - 1.62 default spread + 0.9 x (4.23 ERP + 2.46 CRP), not the section 4 build (13.5-13.8%), and a 20% DDM weight with zero DPS to FY2030 is effectively a terminal-value bet.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose says more than the model: returns-none-of-its-profit and no-dividend-in-the-explicit-window are false because the model pays 50% from FY2031 (DPS Rp16.0-22.6), and the only-conservatism-we- allow claim is contradicted below. The rating is robust: a 50/50 bear/base probability still gives about Rp150, so an asymmetric call is not the issue.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The model reads the deck consistently (IDR rates, 4% g, IDR reporting, BI at 5.75%) and 11.85% matches the small-bank peer cluster (BBMD/BBHI/BSIM/BTPN about 11.8%), but VAL_BANKS pins COE at the 10y yield plus an ERP of 5.0-6.0%; the undisclosed 1.62% default-spread deduction and the separate 4.2% mature ERP plus 2.5% CRP are not reconciled to that card.

conservatism_audit.note: Stack, all small but additive: Q4 provisions Rp485bn vs the Rp453bn annualised 9M run-rate (NP Rp369bn vs about Rp400bn, 8%); 50% payout vs the 56% the assumption text itself derives from g/ROE; 9% vs 10% terminal ROE; 4% terminal growth with 10% ROE and 50% payout implies 5% sustainable g; flat 8.5% NIM against a roughly 2pp compression trend. Together roughly 10-15% of value.

calibration.note: qc returns no unaddressed block, but the three BLOCK justifications are not equally sound (the CIR one is unsupported by S8). The ROE calibration gap of 2.94pp (FY2025A 1.5% vs FY2026E 4.4%) is anchored to the 9M2026 annualised net profit of about Rp400bn, below which the model sits at Rp369bn; the report should state the gate and the Q4 haircut explicitly rather than as an aside.

signoff.notes: Approved. QC PASS, judge PASS, check PASS (facts + lint), no blocking engine flags. The round-1 blocker is resolved: the scenario-wide roe_sustainable override is gone, the justified multiple now uses the model terminal 10.0% at 0.63x and section 4 discloses the constant-multiple convention and its cost to the bull. All FATAL/MATERIAL C1-C7 are answered and accepted. The one carried FIX item, Q1, is text-only: section 4 and the roe basis say the bank must roughly double its 6.2% pre-tax ROE to earn a 13.5% after-tax COE, when the consistent statement is about 2.8x pre-tax (or 4.5% after-tax vs 13.5%); Q1 states no model or target change, and the Rp179 SELL survives either wording. Fix Q1 in the next update; it does not hold sign-off.

bias.note: Base is anchored to the September 2026 actuals (loans Rp13.80trn, DPK Rp17.60trn, CIR 54.16%, PBT Rp385bn) and the FY2026E ROE of 4.51% is the 9M run-rate, not a projection; the two conservative departures (total-asset NIM held at 8.5% while the loan share of assets rises from ~50% to ~64%, zero payout to FY2030E) are disclosed and tied to the last actual or the company's own policy. The constant-multiple convention understates the bull by ~40% (weighted ~1/6) but the SELL survives the correction at ~-35%; the only clear prose error (pre-tax ROE compared with an after-tax COE) errs against the report's own bearish conclusion, so neither direction is distorted.

findings.finding: Section 4, the assumptions roe_sustainable_basis and the extreme_call justification all say the bank 'needs to roughly double its current pre-tax return on equity of 6.2% just to earn its cost of capital'. A 6.23% pre-tax ROE is about 4.8% after tax, and a 13.47% after-tax COE needs ~17.3% pre-tax at the model's 22% tax rate, i.e. roughly 2.8x, not 2x. The sentence compares a pre-tax return with an after-tax cost of equity.

The constant-multiple disclosure is one-sided: the same 0.633x is applied to the bear, whose own terminal ROE is far below 10% on the 6% cost-of-risk path, so the convention overstates the bear at the same time as it understates the bull. The 'about a sixth' lift from correcting the bull is therefore an upper bound on the true correction, not the correction itself.

Section 5, section 6 and the post_bs_review call the 12.13% float 'below the exchange's minimum threshold [S0]', but S0 carries the float, not the listing rule. The house konglo sources stage the rule at 12.5% by 31 March 2027 and 15% by 31 March 2028 for caps above Rp5trn, so the binding near-term gap is 0.37pp, not 2.87pp.

The 10.0% sustainable ROE is the FY2035E point on a path still rising about 0.5pp a year (8.77% FY2032E, 9.27% FY2033E, 9.76% FY2034E) with CAR still near 25% at the horizon, so it is the endpoint of the model, not a converged steady state. Section 4 labels it the terminal-year return but does not say the return has not yet normalised.
